predicted_event_text: Volkswagen reported on October 10, 2025, that global sales of its mid-size gas vehicles rose 5% in September compared to the previous month, as consumers shifted from electric models amid slow charging infrastructure expansion. The automaker attributed the uptick to promotional offers on high-margin gasoline SUVs and sedans in North America and Europe. Separately, Ford announced a temporary increase in production of its best-selling gas models at its Michigan plants, citing robust demand. Industry analysts noted that the trend may pressure automakers to reconsider ambitious EV targets, as lower-cost gas vehicles continue to attract budget-conscious buyers. Meanwhile, VW confirmed it would extend production of its gas-powered Passat and Tiguan models beyond previous timelines, aligning with its updated regional demand forecasts.

On October 3, 2025, Honda Motor Co. announced it will reduce production of mid-size gasoline vehicles at its North American plants by approximately 15% through year-end, citing persistent inventory buildup and softer-than-expected demand in the U.S. market. The move comes after August data showed U.S. output of 88,056 units (93.9% of last year) and overall Honda global production falling for 13 consecutive months. Separately, Volkswagen confirmed it will extend the temporary production pause at its Emden plant by an additional week, now lasting until mid-October, as weak European EV demand continues to weigh on overall output. Both automakers are reassigning some assembly lines to focus on hybrid models, which have seen stronger consumer interest amid slow EV adoption and high fuel prices.

On October 5, 2025, General Motors reported a slight uptick in US sales of mid-size gas vehicles for September, driven by increased fleet orders and promotional financing offers. The company noted that consumer demand for gasoline-powered models remained resilient despite ongoing industry shifts toward electrification. GM also highlighted plans to introduce advanced efficiency features in its 2026 gas lineup to comply with upcoming fuel economy standards. Separately, Ford announced a temporary production adjustment at its Kentucky truck plant, citing parts shortages, though it assured that output of its popular F-series gas models would continue without major disruption.

On October 20, 2025, Nexperia announced it had initiated formal talks with US and Chinese trade officials to address export restrictions affecting its chip supply, warning that prolonged restrictions could disrupt automotive production chains. BMW confirmed its third-quarter production continued as planned but noted it is monitoring inventory levels closely as chip buffers diminish. Mercedes-Benz stated it is assessing alternative suppliers, while Volkswagen reiterated no immediate impact. Industry analysts noted that the dispute underscores broader vulnerabilities in the European automotive sector amid weak demand and tariff pressures.

On October 21, 2025, Stellantis issued a statement cautioning that its European production could face disruptions in the coming weeks unless the Nexperia chip supply issue is resolved, following similar warnings from the ACEA. The automaker confirmed it is exploring alternative chip sources and coordinating with suppliers to mitigate any impact on vehicle output. Stellantis emphasized that while current production continues, the uncertainty around Nexperia deliveries poses a risk for November scheduling. Separately, Ford Europe announced a temporary reduction in shifts at its Cologne EV plant, partly to manage component inventories amid the broader semiconductor uncertainties. These moves come as the industry continues to monitor diplomatic exchanges between the EU, Netherlands, and China regarding the export restrictions on Nexperia.

On October 22, 2025, the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) issued a statement urging EU officials to fast-track semiconductor supply chain diversification, as the Nexperia dispute continues to threaten chip availability for basic automotive components. Several member automakers, including BMW and Mercedes-Benz, reported no immediate production halts but noted they are actively seeking alternative chip suppliers across Asia and Europe. ACEA warned that without a swift resolution, the disruption could compound existing losses from weak demand and tariff pressures in the fourth quarter. Separately, Ford confirmed it will idle its Dearborn F-150 Lightning line until late January 2026, prioritizing gasoline Super Duty production to offset the Novelis aluminum shortage, and projected a $700 million hit to adjusted earnings for the year.

On October 23, 2025, Ford Motor Company issued a profit warning for the fourth quarter, estimating up to $1 billion in lost earnings due to the Novelis aluminum mill fire and persistent semiconductor shortages. The automaker will further reduce F-150 Lightning production and prioritize gasoline-powered trucks. Meanwhile, the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) urged EU governments to mediate the Nexperia chip dispute, warning that continued supply uncertainty could force temporary plant closures. GM Canada announced it will open consultations with Unifor and local officials to evaluate the future of the Cami plant, with options including retooling for a new internal-combustion model amid weak EV demand and trade tariff risks.

Honda announced on October 24 that it is temporarily reducing production at two North American plants due to Nexperia chip shortages, affecting approximately 10,000 vehicles. The automaker cited weeks-long delivery delays from Nexperia and is accelerating sourcing from Texas Instruments and other suppliers. Ford separately warned that its gasoline F-150 production could face cuts by mid-November if the Novelis aluminum supply does not resume sooner than anticipated. Volkswagen reported it has secured alternative chip supplies through spot purchases but cautioned that margins are under pressure. ACEA reiterated calls for EU-China talks to resolve Nexperia's export restrictions, noting that assembly lines face compounding risks from aluminum and semiconductor disruptions.

On October 29, 2025, Volkswagen Group issued a profit warning, citing the escalating Nexperia chip supply disruption. The automaker said that without a swift resolution, it may be forced to temporarily idle production at several European plants within two weeks. Volkswagen noted that alternative chip sources, such as Texas Instruments, are being explored but will take months to ramp up. The warning follows similar concerns from GM and ACEA, as chip stocks dwindle across the industry. Volkswagen's stock fell 4% on the announcement, and the company revised its 2025 operating margin target downward. The European auto association reiterated calls for immediate government intervention to prevent broader manufacturing stoppages.

On November 3, 2025, Stellantis announced a temporary 10% reduction in production of its mid-size gasoline models across North American plants, citing the ongoing semiconductor shortage from Nexperia. The company's cross-functional war room identified priority vehicle allocations, leading to slower assembly of certain gas-powered SUVs and sedans. Honda confirmed its production cuts for the month would remain in effect, while Volkswagen warned that assembly line stoppages for popular gas models could occur within two weeks if alternative legacy chip supplies are not secured. The European Automobile Manufacturers Association urged coordinated sourcing efforts among automakers to mitigate further disruptions. No progress was reported from diplomatic channels regarding Nexperia's chip export restrictions.

On November 12, 2025, Stellantis disclosed that its "war room" has been unable to secure alternative supplies for the legacy chips blocked by the Nexperia dispute, and the company expects to temporarily idle several North American assembly lines within two weeks. CEO Carlos Tavares warned that the disruptions could reduce fourth-quarter production by roughly 20,000 vehicles. Separately, Honda announced it will extend reduced production schedules at two Japanese plants until late November. The European Automobile Manufacturers Association reiterated that chip stocks are critically low, with no immediate resolution in sight from ongoing diplomatic talks between the Netherlands and China. Meanwhile, Volkswagen reaffirmed its commitment to its joint venture with Horizon Robotics, stating the in-house chip development is part of a broader strategy to localize key components and mitigate future supply-chain risks.

On [next date after 2025-11-06], General Motors reported third-quarter earnings, with net income falling 12% year-over-year due to Nexperia chip supply constraints and higher logistics costs. The automaker's global production was cut by roughly 40,000 units during the quarter, but CEO Mary Barra noted that talks between the U.S. and China on semiconductor trade have shown "cautious progress." GM's adjusted operating margin in North America slipped to 8.1%, while its China joint venture posted a small profit. Barra reiterated plans to source legacy chips from Texas Instruments and other alternative suppliers, but warned that full normalization may take until mid-2026. Separately, Ford confirmed it would provide a similar earnings update next week.

On November 10, 2025, the European Automobile Manufacturers Association issued a cautiously optimistic statement that semiconductor supply pressures are beginning to ease, following reports from China that export restrictions on legacy chips from Nexperia’s Dongguan plant have been relaxed. Industry officials note that while full production normalization remains weeks away, the partial resumption of shipments has allowed several automakers, including Volkswagen and Stellantis, to avoid imminent assembly-line stoppages. Separately, Honda confirmed it will maintain reduced shifts at its Celaya, Mexico plant through mid-November but has not yet announced a date for full restoration. The announcement tempered earlier concerns about deepening production cuts, though the European Automobile Manufacturers Association reiterated the need for long-term semiconductor sovereignty. The update offered a first sign of stabilization in the crisis that has disrupted global auto output since late September.

On November 10, 2025, Honda Motor announced it is resuming full production at its Celaya, Mexico plant after receiving restored chip shipments from Nexperia, following the recent U.S.-China agreement. The company raised its full-year profit forecast by ¥50 billion from the prior ¥300 billion, citing improved supply stability and strong North American sales. However, Honda cautioned that U.S. tariffs and currency fluctuations continue to pressure margins. Separately, Volkswagen reiterated its commitment to developing in-house assisted driving chips for China through the CARIAD-Horizon Robotics joint venture, aiming to insulate its business from future trade disruptions. The European Automobile Manufacturers Association urged governments to stabilize semiconductor trade policies, warning that the current case-by-case export system for chips remains fragile. No further assembly stoppages were reported across major automakers as supply gradually normalizes.

On November 12, 2025, Honda announced it will accelerate localization of chip sourcing and production for its North American operations, aiming to mitigate ongoing tariff and supply chain disruptions. CEO Toshihiro Mibe stated the company plans to invest an additional ¥50 billion in semiconductor partnerships and expand in-house design capabilities, targeting a 30% reduction in external chip dependency by 2027. The move follows the recent Nexperia supply uncertainty and the impact of U.S. tariffs, which contributed to a 37% profit drop in the first half of the fiscal year. Honda also confirmed it is evaluating further production adjustments in Mexico and the U.S., though no immediate plant closures were announced. The company reiterated its commitment to maintaining North American sales growth while navigating what it called a "volatile geopolitical environment."

On November 13, 2025, Honda announced a strategic partnership with a Southeast Asian battery supplier to localize EV production and reduce exposure to US tariffs and chip disruptions. The company will co-develop compact EVs for the ASEAN market, aiming to regain share lost to BYD. Operating losses in its automotive division continue, and Honda reaffirmed its reduced full-year forecast. Separately, Volkswagen confirmed that Nexperia chip deliveries have stabilized for now, but warned that long-term supply remains tied to US-China trade talks. BMW reported that US demand remains strong, offsetting weakness in China, and reiterated its cautious 2025 outlook. The chip shortage continues to affect production flexibility across the industry, with no immediate resolution in sight.

On November 15, 2025, Honda announced it would accelerate development of in-house chip capabilities to reduce dependence on external suppliers like Nexperia, following the production disruptions at its Celaya plant. The company reported that the chip shortage and U.S. tariffs had cut global vehicle output by an additional 50,000 units in early November, deepening its third straight quarterly loss in the automotive division. Honda also confirmed it had secured limited chip supplies from alternative sources to restart Mexican production by late November, but warned that full recovery depends on stable U.S.-China trade relations. Meanwhile, Ford CEO Jim Farley reiterated that supply chain resilience remains the top priority, hinting at planned investments in domestic rare earth processing facilities.

On November 25, 2025, Honda announced it will accelerate development of a new hybrid mid-size sedan for the Southeast Asian market, aiming to counter declining sales amid rising Chinese competition. The move follows Honda’s reduced full-year profit outlook and a 30% retail sales drop in Indonesia. Honda’s Chief Operating Officer cited the need to adapt to supply chain pressures from chip shortages and U.S. tariffs, which have forced production adjustments in North America. The hybrid sedan is expected to launch in late 2026, leveraging existing components to minimize new investment. Honda also confirmed it will maintain its current Mexico plant closure until chip supply stabilizes, but will resume production of its popular City model in Thailand next month. No further layoffs or plant shutdowns were announced.

On November 25, 2025, Honda announced a strategic shift to consolidate its mid-size gas vehicle lineup in Southeast Asia, citing persistent losses from its automotive division. The company plans to phase out two underperforming sedan models and focus on the updated City sedan, while delaying further EV investments in the region. This move comes after Honda cut its full-year profit outlook by a fifth and reported a third straight quarterly operating loss in its automotive division. The decision reflects ongoing pressures from Chinese EV competition and a chip shortage that reduced vehicle sales by 110,000 units. Separately, Ford reiterated its commitment to mid-size gas trucks, with CEO Jim Farley stating the company will prioritize supply chain resilience and domestic sourcing for critical materials.

On December 2, 2025, Volkswagen announced a €2 billion joint venture with STMicroelectronics to design and produce automotive-grade chips for its global vehicle lineup, targeting a 2027 production start. The move is part of the broader diversification push prompted by the Nexperia crisis and Beijing's export restrictions. Volkswagen's CEO said the partnership will reduce reliance on Chinese semiconductors for critical safety and infotainment systems. Separately, BMW disclosed a 12% drop in November deliveries in its core Chinese market, attributing the decline to ongoing trade tensions and consumer shift toward domestic EVs. BMW reiterated plans to expand battery sourcing from European suppliers like Northvolt. Mercedes-Benz also reported a quarterly loss in its Chinese joint venture, citing weak demand and higher raw material costs. The German automakers continue to balance cost pressures with emissions targets.

On December 9, 2025, Volkswagen Group reported a 15% drop in Q4 profit, citing ongoing supply chain costs from Chinese semiconductor restrictions and aluminum shortages. CEO Oliver Blume stated that the company is accelerating its "China+1" strategy, increasing investment in non-Chinese chip suppliers and securing raw material agreements in Australia and South America. Meanwhile, Ford confirmed it will restart F-150 Lightning production in mid-2026, after the aluminum plant resumes operations. Ford also announced a new joint venture with a U.S. rare earth processor to reduce foreign dependence, aligning with CEO Jim Farley’s previous warnings. The moves come as U.S. and EU regulators continue to pressure automakers to diversify supply chains, and as Chinese EV makers expand market share in Europe.

On December 5, 2025, Ford announced it will extend the production pause for the F-150 Lightning through early 2026 as the key aluminum supplier remains offline until Q1. The company also revised its 2025 earnings guidance downward, citing the supply disruption and weaker EV demand following the expiration of federal tax credits. Separately, Hyundai confirmed plans to increase hybrid vehicle output by 30% in 2026, aiming to offset declining EV sales and leverage strong hybrid demand trends. The moves reflect automakers' ongoing adjustments to supply chain constraints and shifting consumer preferences.

On 2025-12-10, BMW Group announced plans to invest 80 billion euros through 2030, a reduction from its previous five-year plan, as the automaker grapples with declining sales in China and rising costs from EU emission regulations. CFO Walter Mertl stated the company will prioritize localizing production in key markets, including a new battery assembly plant in the United States, and increase sourcing of non-Chinese semiconductors. The strategy mirrors Volkswagen’s recent belt-tightening and reflects broader pressure on German automakers to reduce dependency on China while managing weak domestic demand and intensified competition from Chinese EV makers expanding in Europe. BMW also confirmed it will deepen its software partnership with Chinese firm Momenta but retain control over core platform development.

On December 12, 2025, Ford Motor Company announced that it would temporarily reduce production of its mid-size gas-powered sedans and SUVs at two U.S. plants due to ongoing semiconductor shortages and a fire-related supply disruption at a key aluminum supplier. The company stated that inventory of popular gas models like the Ford Fusion and Explorer remained below normal levels, but it expected to ramp up output in early 2026 after securing alternative chip sources through a new partnership announced under the JPMorgan-led national security initiative. Meanwhile, Hyundai reported that its mid-size gas vehicle sales in November 2025 declined 4%, as the automaker prioritized hybrid production to meet shifting consumer demand. The announcements underscored continued supply chain stress for traditional gas vehicles amid the broader industry pivot to electrification and diversification away from Chinese components.

Volkswagen Group announced on December 15, 2025, that it will accelerate efforts to secure alternative rare-earth supplies outside China, following the streamlined export licenses granted to Ford’s suppliers. CEO Oliver Blume stated that while current supplies remain stable, the exclusion of German automakers from the new licenses underscores the need to reduce dependence on Chinese rare earths for electric vehicle magnets. Volkswagen is exploring partnerships with suppliers in Australia and Brazil and may increase investment in recycling technologies. Separately, BMW confirmed it is in talks with several non-Chinese rare-earth producers to diversify its supply chain. The announcements come as European automakers face pressure to secure critical materials amid ongoing US-China trade tensions and potential further export restrictions.

On December 19, 2025, Ford Motor Company confirmed that its key aluminum supplier has resumed full production following the earlier fire, allowing the F-150 Lightning assembly line to return to normal capacity. The company also stated that the new streamlined rare-earth export licenses from China have stabilized its supply chain for critical magnets, preventing further disruptions. However, Ford noted that overall sales in November were still depressed due to the end of federal EV tax credits, and it expects a gradual recovery in 2026. Separately, Hyundai announced plans to expand hybrid production by 30% in the first quarter of next year, capitalizing on rising consumer demand for hybrid models as EV incentives remain absent.

On December 22, 2025, Ford Motor Company issued a statement confirming that its rare-earth magnet supply chain has stabilized following the issuance of general export licenses from China on December 11. CEO Jim Farley noted that the streamlined permits allow Ford to maintain production schedules at its U.S. plants through early 2026, but cautioned that global semiconductor shortages remain a risk. Ford also announced it will accelerate its in-house chip development program, allocating an additional $500 million to a new joint venture with a U.S. semiconductor firm. Separately, Honda Motor extended its December 17 production pause announcement, confirming that output at its Japanese plants will now halt through January 10 due to persistent chip supply constraints. Honda maintained its reduced 2025 sales outlook of 3.34 million units.

On January 15, 2026, Ford Motor Company announced a strategic partnership with a Japanese semiconductor manufacturer to develop and supply advanced chips for its electric and gas vehicle lines. The five-year agreement, valued at over $2 billion, aims to secure a stable supply of chips outside China and reduce reliance on rare-earth magnets from Chinese suppliers. Ford CEO Jim Farley stated the partnership will help insulate the automaker from future geopolitical disruptions, referencing the chip shortage that hit Honda and other rivals in late 2025. The first chips are expected by mid-2026, with initial deployment in Ford's F-150 and Explorer models. The announcement comes amid broader industry efforts to reshore chip production, though analysts note that full capacity will take years to achieve. Separately, Ford reported fourth-quarter earnings that narrowly missed expectations due to lingering supply constraints.

On February 3, 2026, Ford Motor Company reported better-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings, citing improved supply chains for rare-earth magnets following the streamlined export licenses from China. The automaker noted that its production schedules are stabilizing, though it warned that geopolitical tensions remain a risk. Separately, Honda Motor Co. announced it has secured long-term semiconductor supply agreements with multiple non-Japanese and non-Chinese chipmakers, reducing its reliance on Chinese-sourced components. Honda’s operating profit for the quarter was still impacted by the late-2025 production pauses, but executives expressed confidence in a gradual recovery. In its earnings call, Ford also highlighted the ongoing U.S.-China trade uncertainties and the potential for further policy shifts under the Trump administration. The announcements came as the broader auto industry continues to navigate supply-chain realignments and regional policy changes.

On February 25, 2026, Honda Motor Co. announced a strategic pivot to bolster its gasoline-powered vehicle lineup, citing the slower-than-expected EV adoption and ongoing tariff pressures. The company plans to invest ¥120 billion over the next year to refresh its Accord and CR-V models for the North American market, aiming to sustain margins while EV demand remains tepid. Honda also confirmed it will accelerate semiconductor partnerships with Japanese suppliers, aiming to secure stable chip supplies for its gas vehicle production lines. The decision comes amid a broader industry reassessment, as automakers grapple with protectionist trade policies and shifting consumer preferences. Honda reaffirmed its full-year operating profit outlook of ¥550 billion, but analysts expect the gas vehicle push to partially offset mounting EV losses.

On 2026-03-03, Honda Motor Co. unveiled a revised electric vehicle roadmap, announcing plans to delay several new EV models and increase investment in hybrid technology. The shift follows the ¥267.1 billion in EV-related expenses reported last month and a reassessment of strategy amid slowing EV growth and trade frictions. Honda also stated it will prioritize development of in-house chip capabilities and explore joint procurement with other Japanese automakers to mitigate semiconductor supply risks. The announcement came as Honda's motorcycle division continued to offset auto losses, with record sales in emerging markets. Separately, Toyota reported a cautious outlook for North American production due to ongoing US import duty uncertainties.

On March 5, 2026, Honda Motor Co. announced it has secured a memorandum of understanding with a leading Taiwanese semiconductor foundry to develop custom automotive chips for its mid-size gas vehicle lineup. The partnership is part of Honda's broader strategy to diversify its chip supply chain away from China, following the severe shortage that disrupted production in late 2025. The new chips are expected to be integrated into engine control units and infotainment systems for 2027 model year vehicles. Meanwhile, Honda reported that its North American production volumes for mid-size gas models remain stable despite ongoing US import duties, as the company draws down inventory built before the tariffs took effect. The automaker reiterated its full-year operating profit forecast of ¥550 billion, citing stronger-than-expected sales in markets outside North America.

On 2026-03-18, Ford Motor Co. disclosed further details of its Universal EV platform strategy in a regulatory filing, confirming that the platform will underpin a range of models, including a mid-size gas-electric hybrid crossover aimed at the core 8703 segment. The filing noted that the hybrid variant is intended to bridge consumer demand during the EV transition and will feature a conventional gasoline engine paired with a smaller battery pack, targeting a starting price below $28,000. Ford also reiterated that its internal combustion engine lineup, including the Ranger and Explorer, will see incremental updates through 2028. Separately, Honda announced on the same day that it will postpone the launch of its new Pilot generation by six months to reallocate engineering resources to its struggling EV program, a move that traders expect to tighten supply of mid-size gas utility vehicles in North America for the upcoming model year.

On March 10, 2026, Honda Motor Co. issued a statement addressing the persistent vibration issues in the power unit supplied to Aston Martin’s Formula 1 team, following battery failures that jeopardized the Australian Grand Prix. Honda acknowledged the problem, noting that engineering teams are prioritizing a fix before the Japanese Grand Prix, but cautioned that a complete resolution may take several weeks. Separately, the automaker reiterated its commitment to its broader electrification strategy, despite mounting EV-related losses and US tariff headwinds. Honda also confirmed it will provide an updated fiscal-year outlook in its next earnings release, amid ongoing supply chain and trade policy uncertainty. The company’s motorcycle division continues to offset automotive losses with record sales.

On March 20, 2026, Honda provides further details on its strategic pivot following the $15.7 billion EV writedown. The company announces accelerated development of next-generation hybrid powertrains for the U.S. market, with plans to launch a new hybrid mid-size sedan and SUV by late 2027. Honda also confirms it will deepen investments in its India operations to strengthen cost competitiveness, targeting a 30% reduction in hybrid component costs through local sourcing. The shift comes as Honda reports a 40% increase in hybrid sales in March compared to last year, primarily driven by demand for the new Civic Hybrid and CR-V Hybrid. Meanwhile, the fate of the Sony Honda Mobility joint venture remains under review, with no decision expected before mid-2026.

On March 20, 2026, Honda announced a detailed restructuring plan in response to its historic $4.3 billion loss and $15.7 billion EV writedown. The company will close one U.S. assembly plant and halt production at another for six months, shifting those lines to hybrid powertrain assembly. Additionally, Honda will cut 3,000 U.S. salaried positions and renegotiate supplier contracts to reduce costs. In India, Honda plans to expand two existing plants to produce affordable hybrids and small gas vehicles for emerging markets, targeting a 15% market share by 2028. CEO Toshihiro Mibe stated the moves are necessary to stabilize finances while accelerating hybrid development, but warned that further writedowns are possible if U.S. tariffs or Chinese competition intensify. The company also confirmed it will retain its Sony Honda Mobility joint venture but shift its focus to global markets beyond China.

On March 19, 2026, Ford Motor Company reported a preliminary fourth-quarter EBIT loss of $1.7 billion for its Model e division, exceeding previous estimates, as the automaker grapples with the transition to electric vehicles. CEO Jim Farley confirmed that Ford will increase production of its upcoming extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) by 20% to offset weak demand for full battery models. The company also disclosed that it is in advanced talks with a Chinese battery supplier to reduce costs for its Universal EV platform, aiming for the $30,000 target price. Ford’s overall 2025 net income fell 8% due to writedowns on stalled EV projects. Separately, the company announced a $500 million investment to retool its Dearborn plant for hybrid F-150 production, signaling a strategic shift away from full electrification in core truck segments.

On March 25, 2026, Ford Motor Company announced a strategic restructuring of its North American operations in response to persistent tariff pressures and supplier disruptions. The plan includes a temporary reduction in production of its best-selling F-150 and Explorer models to reallocate resources toward hybrid development, aligning with shifting consumer demand. Ford also revealed it is negotiating with a new battery supplier to mitigate reliance on the damaged supply chain. Meanwhile, the company faces a potential SEC investigation into disclosure practices related to its 2025 recall record. CFO John Lawler stated that adjusted free cash flow for the first quarter may fall below the $5–6 billion full-year guidance due to ongoing parts shortages. Ford shares extended their decline, dropping another 3%.

On 2026-03-28, Ford Motor Company announced a downward revision to its 2026 production targets for mid-size gas vehicles in North America, citing sustained tariff-related cost increases and ongoing supply chain disruptions. The automaker now expects to produce 15% fewer mid-size models than initially planned, primarily affecting its popular Fusion and Escape lines. Ford also warned that adjusted free cash flow for the year may fall below the previously guided $5–6 billion range due to higher input costs and logistics delays. The production cuts will spare the company’s hybrid and electric vehicle lines, reflecting a strategic shift to preserve margins on higher-demand models. Ford shares dropped an additional 4% in after-hours trading.

On March 30, 2026, Honda released its fiscal year-end earnings report, officially recording the previously announced $4.3 billion loss—its first in 69 years. The automaker outlined a revised mid-term strategy, including a shift of remaining EV investments to hybrids and plug-in hybrids, and the closure of one underutilized North American assembly plant. CFO Shinji Aoyama stated that Honda will prioritize flexible production lines to adapt to tariff volatility and Chinese competition, but declined to provide a timeline for returning to profitability. Separately, the company confirmed it will not revive the canceled AFEELA project with Sony, leaving Sony Honda Mobility to pursue software-only initiatives. No partner replacement was announced.

In late October 2025, the Chinese Ministry of Commerce publicly expressed strong opposition to the Dutch government's invocation of the Goods Availability Act to control Nexperia, stating it undermines normal international business operations and violates market principles. The ministry signaled it would explore all options to safeguard Chinese companies' legitimate rights and interests, including potential diplomatic negotiations and trade measures. Meanwhile, Wingtech Technology's legal team filed preliminary motions in Dutch courts challenging the government's decision, arguing procedural irregularities and insufficient evidence of security threats. Nexperia continued its regular chip production under state supervision, with no immediate impact on supply chains for automotive and industrial customers. The European Commission declined to comment, citing ongoing bilateral discussions between the Netherlands and China.

On October 20, 2025, the Chinese Ministry of Commerce summoned the Dutch ambassador to formally protest the Dutch government's invocation of the Goods Availability Act against Nexperia, warning of retaliatory measures if the matter is not resolved. Meanwhile, the China Semiconductor Industry Association issued a follow-up statement urging member companies to reduce reliance on Dutch-origin doped electronic materials. Nexperia’s management informed key automotive and industrial clients that while operations continue, long-term supply stability for HS4 3818 products remains uncertain due to governance restrictions. Wingtech’s legal team confirmed preparations for a complaint under EU investment treaties, though no formal filing has been made. The crisis has dampened investor sentiment, with Wingtech’s shares falling an additional 5% on the Shenzhen exchange.

On 2025-12-01, Nexperia's Chinese parent Wingtech Technology released its preliminary Q4 2025 financial results, revealing a 3.5% sequential revenue decline in its semiconductor division due to operational uncertainty at the seized Dutch unit. The company reiterated its commitment to legal and diplomatic channels while noting it had initiated contingency plans to shift some production capacity to its other manufacturing sites in Asia. Wingtech's CFO stated that the dispute had added approximately €45 million in legal and advisory costs during the quarter. Separately, Nexperia's interim Dutch management announced it would proceed with a scheduled upgrade of its Nijmegen wafer fab, funded by existing cash reserves, and said it remained in informal dialogue with Chinese suppliers to ensure raw material continuity for specialty doped substrates. The Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs declined to comment on ongoing talks.

On an unspecified date after October 30, 2025, Wingtech Technology released its third-quarter 2025 financial results, reporting a 4.8% sequential decline in semiconductor revenue, which it attributed to operational uncertainty at its seized Dutch subsidiary Nexperia. The company warned that full-year revenue would likely miss earlier guidance if the Dutch government does not restore management control by year-end. Wingtech reiterated that it is pursuing legal remedies and seeking support from Chinese authorities. Separately, Nexperia issued a statement saying production continues under state supervision, but noted that some customers have delayed orders due to supply-chain concerns. The Dutch government acknowledged ongoing talks with Wingtech but offered no timeline for resolution.

On November 10, 2025, the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) issued a statement warning that the ongoing Dutch government seizure of Nexperia could disrupt supplies of doped electronic materials critical for automotive production by early 2026 if no resolution is reached. ACEA urged both sides to engage in constructive dialogue to avoid exacerbating the chip shortage. Meanwhile, Wingtech Technology reported a preliminary third-quarter semiconductor revenue increase of 12.2% year-on-year, but cautioned that the dispute may pressure fourth-quarter results if the control transfer is not reversed. The Dutch government reiterated its commitment to finding a balanced solution while maintaining national security measures.

On December 2, 2025, Wingtech Technology announced that Nexperia has resumed partial operations after the Dutch government's suspension of control, allowing the chipmaker to restart production of legacy semiconductors for the automotive industry. Wingtech cautioned that full normalization depends on ongoing negotiations between Beijing and The Hague. In response, the China Semiconductor Industry Association welcomed the suspension as a step toward resolving supply chain disruptions but reiterated calls for a permanent resolution. Meanwhile, several automakers, including Toyota and European manufacturers, reported improved chip availability in recent weeks, easing previous production constraints. The Dutch economy minister confirmed that talks with Chinese authorities continue, focusing on ensuring stable supplies of doped electronic materials without compromising regulatory safeguards.

On November 25, 2025, Nexperia announced it had resumed full production of doped electronic materials (HS4 3818) at its Dutch facilities following the government's suspension of control. The company stated that supply to automotive clients, including Toyota, had normalized, alleviating earlier production concerns. Wingtech Technology reported a stabilization in revenue and profit, citing the resumption of cross-border chip flows. However, the statement noted that long-term regulatory clarity remains under discussion between Dutch and Chinese officials. Economy Minister Vincent Karremans confirmed ongoing negotiations to establish a permanent framework for Nexperia's operations, emphasizing the need to balance security and supply chain reliability. Industry analysts said the pause had prevented further disruption to legacy chip supplies but warned that deeper geopolitical risks persist.

On November 25, 2025, Nexperia announced a temporary shift in production strategy, moving some assembly lines for high-demand doped electronic materials from its Chinese unit to third-party facilities in Southeast Asia, aiming to mitigate supply risks pending a diplomatic resolution. The Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs welcomed the move as a constructive step, while cautioning that regulatory oversight under the Goods Availability Act remains in force. In China, the Ministry of Commerce reiterated its call for a pragmatic solution, noting that dialogue channels remain open. Automakers, including Toyota, reported that chip stocks have stabilized in recent days, but stressed that long-term security requires a sustainable political framework. No further government seizures or export bans have been reported.

On December 3, 2025, major automakers reported worsening chip supply disruptions tied to the Nexperia crisis, prompting several to launch contingency plans for basic semiconductor production. Companies including Stellantis and Volkswagen announced they would begin developing their own low-tech chips in-house to reduce dependence on Nexperia’s Chinese plant, which remains a bottleneck. Meanwhile, Nexperia’s Dutch headquarters confirmed it was in ongoing talks with Chinese regulators about resuming finished-chip exports, though no timeline was given. Economists warned that the standoff could trigger profit warnings among auto suppliers in early 2026, as the industry struggles to adapt to geopolitical supply-chain risks.
